India Oṃ! Salutations to the one who has brought an end to the lineage of Māyā, the two skeletons, and the devourer of time.
Beyond the sky, without appearance, and devoid of vibration and bliss. || 1 ||

O you who have made all objects of perception the object of perception, yet have cast aside the state of being without an object; O you who have emerged from the exhaustion of both virtues and faults, you are an ocean of power.
Unshakable, partless, pure, and beyond bliss, he is Bhairava;
he is the void, the void, and likewise the void, the intermediate space between the void and the non-void. || 3 ||
It is non-empty within all existents, the cause of dissolution and origination; it transcends the cultivation of the graspable object, and is devoid of the senses. (4)
The infinite self, whose nature is the pervasion of space, is the negation of all existents;
it is liberated from waking and dreaming, moving within the state of deep sleep.
Beyond the fourth state is the supreme limit; that limit is the Supreme Śiva.
The Lord is established everywhere, transcending all measures, and perfectly pure.
It is free from existence and non-existence, liberated and unassailed by doubt;
it transcends the means of valid cognition and conventional trust, and is devoid of coming and going.
O Lord of gods, sovereign of all, tell me everything without exception, O Master.
I have a great doubt, O Māyādhva, concerning that which has been heard— this "Indra’s net" with its many divisions and hidden meanings.
Therein indeed [he taught] the final doctrine, the remainder, the divisions of knowledge, the Kula tradition,
the profundity of the meaning of mantras, and likewise the profundity of the meaning of the principles (tattvas).
"I do not understand the meaning of words according to grammar, syntax, and logic;
O Lord, my intellect is deluded, having been led astray by many servants. (11)
O Lord of Gods, by what means is the true nature of reality to be known—that by which it is truly understood, free from hypocrisy and illusion? (12)
[He was worshipped] by Nandin, Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and others, by the hosts of Ṛṣis and Yoginīs,
by the sages, by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and likewise by the groups of Indra and Sūrya.
"The supreme state has been described, yet that state which is not known [to others] exists as something even greater than that; so we say, O leader of the Asuras. (14)
O God, I am your constant devotee in deed, mind, and speech;
please grant me grace by means of a concise method through which one is liberated.

Knowledge that is free from exertion, devoid of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), liberated from concentration and meditation (dhāraṇā-dhyāna), and not scorched by the reasoning of yoga and the like; || 16 ||

O Lord of the World, you who are gracious-souled and affectionate toward your devotees, tell me this: [what is the fate of one] devoid of vows, sacrifices, and ritual acts, inactive, and shunned by holy places? (17)
Listen with one-pointed attention to that which is the supreme reality;
it has never been told, O blessed lady, even by a guru or by Śukra himself. (18)
Likewise, for the sequence of Gaṇeśa, there is indeed Bhuṅginanda;
it is hidden from all scriptures, occurring when the Fire (Śikhin) is situated upon the Stone (Pāśāṇa).
Just as one who is hidden or concealed is still perceived when not separated from his companion, so too, O Śiva, the immeasurable is both seen and yet not seen. (20)
Just as fire, by force, enters into the midst of water and, through its connection with the interior of a vessel, becomes hidden within; || 21 ||
In that same way, Śiva is all-pervading, abiding like the appearance of space;
as oil is in a sesame seed and shade in a tree, so He resides within the Kula in the state of deep sleep.
Like a crest on the head, or like a bamboo, a tongue, or a plank,
that which is rich with variegated wings is not seen at all once the vapor has vanished.
But where rock salt is situated in the midst of pure water, its form cannot be seen, being devoid of taste. (24)
The seed of a banyan tree is in the banyan; lead is in the inner gold;
the six flavors are in the portion of the earth; and the means for obtaining the colors are in space.
In that same way, [one attains] Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, who is peaceful and characterized by the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva). || 26 ||
O Mahādeva, ignorance is most wonderful, great, and difficult to endure;
by what means is He, who is free from all limiting adjuncts, accessible? (27)
"O Lord, it is clear to me that there is no grasping of that [object] here on earth;
for by knowing which, O Destroyer of Tripura, true satisfaction arises. (28)
Abandoning silence, speak words that lead to great prosperity.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīparamarahasya*, in the *Niruttaravāda*, which has emerged from the stream of Bhairava’s hearing, in the *Tade* [or *Tadeda*] section.
The venerable [teacher] said:
I shall speak according to reality, free from deceptive knowledge; having abandoned delusion and error, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp the supreme state. (1)
The bath performed with the internal organs within the state of meditation is liberated even in the five [elements] and so forth;
the mind devoid of thought is "no-mind" (niścitta), the supreme state. (2)
Together with the praśānta breaths, such as kumbha, pūraka,
and recaka, he [performed] ten thousand sets of the ten vital airs (vāyu).
Each of these, however, consists of a thousandfold nature; Prāṇa and the others, O Dhanañjaya, are established within the flow of ten thousand channels, situated in the midst of the Kula.
Abandon the multitude of vital airs as well as the multitude of principles;
renounce the great fortress of the web of mantras and the web of ritual actions.
Abandon entirely, like straw, the multitude of scriptures with their manifold meanings;
[focus instead on] the six chakras, the sixteen supports, the three targets, and the five voids.
Having abandoned the station of the *lakṣa* as well as the tip of the *ghaṇṭikā*,
one should likewise abandon the multitude of seventy-two thousand channels.
What is the use of pressing the bladder? What is the fruit of the pleasure of the penis?
When the wheel (cakra) arises from the bliss of grasping, [the goddess] Klinnā is indeed produced by that pressing.
In that state, for those who have attained the fruit, there is nothing consisting solely of bondage; rather, at that time, it is revealed to them through the bliss of union with the Yoginīs.
At that time, I spoke of the bliss residing in the womb, which consists of the essence of wine, intoxicated with passion, and free from waves.
At that time, I spoke for the sake of vision regarding Nanda, who is beyond old age;
however, there is something further beyond that, where no further creation arises.
It is neither the bliss of power (śakti), nor the bliss of non-bliss, nor indeed the bliss of Śiva;
it is a bliss devoid of [all] bliss, abiding like one in deep sleep.
Beyond the senses and not an object of perception, the all-pervading Sadāśiva is free from the cognitive faculties and devoid of both time and non-time. || 13 ||
Neither mind nor intellect exists, nor does the ego-sense; there is neither means of knowledge nor object of knowledge, and neither quality nor defect. (14)
There is neither goodness (sattva), nor passion (rajas), nor darkness (tamas), nor even the [spiritual] stages (bhūmi);
there is no caste (varṇa) among those born into castes, nor is there any song (geya) regarding sensations and the like. || 15 ||
O Dear One, they say it is neither logic, nor the movement through the channels, nor devoid of ritual action and dharma; it is neither the moon, nor the sun, nor even fire.
Neither by those with their winds calmed, nor by one on earth, nor by one moving in the atmosphere;
neither by a yakṣa nor by a lord of nāgas can he be overcome—he who is devoid of both merit and demerit. (17)
There was no one who was humpbacked, nor anyone with deformed hands; there was nothing inferior or superior.
Neither seed, nor forest tree, nor medicinal herb was lacking. (18)
Whether it be a taste or an elixir, neither long nor short,
one is not stained by comings and goings, for its flow is uninterrupted.
Empty, empty, so too empty is the state devoid of bliss;
it is liberated from the bliss of women and corrupted by the bliss of sense objects. (20)
It is a dense thicket of intense bliss for those whose minds are pure with joy;
it is intoxicated by the essence of the bliss of the void and overflowing with the bliss of awakening. || 21 ||
The state of blissless peace, Nirvana which is the end of sense objects;
situated in the void, abiding in the form of the void, having the nature of the void, and originating from the void.
He who knows that Lord— who consists of the five voids, who is beginningless, immutable, and the Creator— whose creation remains established even at the end, is a knower of reality.
Indeed, one should observe its middle, end, and beginning as being unified;
thus, action, knowledge, and will proceed without interruption. (24)
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon the notion of death;
for the physical body (piṇḍa) comes from that very source and returns to that very place.
The entire universe has arisen from the power-source (śaktivila) of the abode of emptiness;
it indeed dissolves back into that very place, where there is a reunion once again. (26)
One should not be defiled by unions, for the stream [of existence] is uninterrupted;
indeed, everything was originally entirely [undifferentiated], and afterwards the process of creation proceeds.
Furthermore, they dissolve right there; how can that middle state be considered a firm support?
From Śiva the body is produced, and into Śiva the body returns again. (28)
From the agitation of power (śakti) arises the body (piṇḍa), and from its non-agitation, that which has the form of the void;
it is beyond the reach of the senses, all-pervading, and both supreme and non-supreme.
Therefore, Śakti has emerged forth as the awakener of the wheel of the Mātṛkās;
by the abandonment of Śiva and Śakti, there is neither the body nor the binding of the body.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, dissolves into the Void;
when everything dissolves therein, that state is designated as the Liṅga. || 31 ||
The mind is the sign, the power of consciousness is the vibration born from the root of the *kanda*;
for he who constantly meditates upon this triad as being one in a single place [attains success]. (32)
He is liberated from all bonds, stainless like the sky; he is not defiled by sin through action, mind, or speech. (33)
Having meditated upon Śiva as omnipresent, who would not be liberated from bondage?
The entire universe has Śiva as its essence; whatever action there is, that has Śiva as its essence. (34)
Whatever is conceptual construction is the terrible weapon; whatever is purity is known as the Supreme (Parā).
That which is impure is always Ucchuṣmā; that which is mixed is Bhairava. (35)
That which is wine is Mārtāṇḍa, and that which is liquor is known as Umā;
these five substances, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śiva, have been proclaimed. (36)
"I am not impure; here I am, presided over by the five elements—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself. (37)
The nose, the eyes, the ears, the mouth, and the penis as the fifth—these impurities are indeed in the lower part [of the body], while the lamp is always above. (38)
One sees, moves about constantly, hears, rejoices, and touches;
these five deities are established in the root *kulaliṅga*. (39)
Flesh, blood, as well as bones, sinews, marrow, and impurity;
semen, phlegm, hair of the head, and whatever other [substances] are in the continuity of the limbs. (40)

From the twice-born and others down to the barbarians (mlecchas), and according to the number of cows, horses, and other animals, that supreme reality is directly present there—even specifically within grass and wood. (41)
Likewise, the names of the ten winds by enumeration are:
Sūryānanda, Rasānanda, Samānanda, and from Udāna [the fourth]. (42)
Vyānānanda, Janānanda, Kūrmānanda, and Kṛkodara;
then Ahaṅkāra as the ninth, and Dhanañjaya as the tenth. (43)
The power of the Lord of Prāṇa and Apāna obstructs the anus in the apāna;
in every direction along the path of the deities, the eight beginning with Brahmā are proclaimed. (44)
Akalarka, Amala, Caṇḍa, Puṇḍra, Vātapa, Nandin, Pavana, who has Yama as his presiding deity, and Śaṅkara is remembered as the eighth. || 45 ||
In the *samāna* breath she is named *samanā*; in the *apāna* she abides as *unmanī*.
In the *vyāna* she is the goddess *cakrakī*, and in the *nāga* she is the supreme *bhujagī*.
In the *kūrma* [vāyu], the power is contracted; in the *kṛkara*, it carries out actions;
in the *devadatta*, it is characterized by egoism; and in the *dhanañjaya*, it is of eternal form. (47)
The ten eternal powers (nityā-śaktis) reside in the midst of the wind, supported by space;
and seventy-two million others reside sequentially in the navel-cakra.
But in the center, Bhairava himself, the teacher of the world, appearing like the sky, free from affliction and supremely void, shines resplendent in the middle of the navel. 49.
The secret lotus, being constantly enjoyed, is established as Kālarudra; protecting the head and the *piṇḍa*, it expands for the sake of diversion. (50)
The Lord consists of all the channels (nāḍīs), with the lines of body hair forming its folds;
it possesses a thousand, a hundred thousand, and ten million rays, serving as the lamp of the power of will (icchā-śakti).
Invisible, the support of the world, the body situated within the body; though one, it delights [all] through manifold universal forms. 52.
And this is not to be obtained here by asceticism, nor by gifts;
it is obtained through the application of the Guru’s mouth, as revealed everywhere.
Otherwise, one wanders through millions of scriptures and does not find the supreme,
peaceful, and utterly pure tradition accompanied by its oral instruction.
One whose self is disciplined by the oral tradition and endowed with pure disposition attains a stainless state,
free from intoxication and deceit.

But if Śambhu should be pleased, and if [further] birth does not exist, then, having obtained it from the position of the Guru, one should cause it to be known through the transmission from mouth to mouth. (56)
One should cause the Lord, in whose heart the universe resides, to be directly perceived through the application of meditative disposition and by the exhaustion of merit and demerit. 57.
O Goddess, having destroyed conceptual construction, the Guru should establish [the disciple] in that state.
Knowing Śiva to be present in every condition, who would not be liberated from bondage? || 58 ||
O supreme leader, if you, with a serene soul, are not distressed by me—being yourself free from limiting conditions and devoid of a self, and liberated from action and its cause. (59)
What is the means? By what measure should Kulabhairava cause [the disciple] to grasp it?
For the mind has entered within the body; it is flickering and likewise restless. (60)
By means of which there may arise unwavering stability through this instruction, and by the mere realization of which your doubts are severed. (61)
Neither bound nor yet liberated, and certainly not one who liberates the bound—if the universe were essentially bound, then one would attain liberation. (62)
The Supreme Lord is independent and liberated from all bonds;
he appears bound only by his own conceptual construction, for there is indeed no bondage for Śiva.
O beautiful one, Śiva, Śakti, and the Self exist in a state of oneness;
for him there is no bondage whatsoever, because Śiva is all-pervasive in every respect.
O Goddess of gods, I have also taught bondage and liberation, which differentiate the three principles and possess the form of reality; yet, one who is not bound is not liberated.
In every treatise, I have spoken [of this], yet it has been concealed from the perspective of the ultimate truth; it is a most terrible intimidation, bringing fear of hell and other such states. (66)
O beautiful one, this has been told to you for the sake of the creation and preservation [of the world].
All that was previously spoken is entirely Śiva, who is omnipresent. (67)
O Goddess, doubt shall persist only so long as one does not find the reality;
once this supreme reality is known, one moves about like the wind. 68.
That which is called "bondage" is merely a designation; it is a non-perception, a fruitless entity.
Everything is composed of Śiva, O auspicious lady—this has been proclaimed by you again and again. (69)
That which is the will to see and that which is non-will—these two states, pure and impure—are the will consisting of Sadāśiva; beyond that, there is no action, for he is Śiva.
O sinless one, ritual action is auspicious; there is always a distinction between actions, yet they are one.
For by whichever path it may be, it is perceived in such a manner.
Therefore, for you who follow this path, there is no bondage, as you are of the nature of Śiva.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīparamarahasya*, within the *Niruttaravāda* concerning the stream of sound.
The Goddess said:
"Tell the truth, O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord who brings an end to suffering."
By the mere knowledge of which there is no further transmigration. || 1 ||
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
I shall proclaim it to you, so listen with a one-pointed mind, my dear. 2.
Through the application of many beans [i.e., trivialities], the scripture has been corrupted by the [pseudo-]scripture;
it is characterized by conduct devoted to much disputing due to mutual contradictions. || 3 ||
And this instruction on many scriptures was composed by me for the sake of sport;
however, O Goddess, when I devour a man alone in the vicinity of a family [or clan], [this is for his benefit].
Then, during the three sacrifices, various scriptures were composed;
the Supreme Lord, though solitary, sports together with Śakti.
That Lord Kāmeśvara, who is the cause of both arising and dissolution, has himself perceived his own form; likewise, he reveals that which is formless.
The wheel of mantras and the wheel of yogis are surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions; there is but one God and no other—what need is there for duality? (7)
For what purpose indeed was the division of the scriptures made, or what is the sequence of rules for duality?
You have taught everything as non-dual; O Great Lord, duality does not exist.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"In the practice of non-duality, indeed, duality is perceived today;
just as when a seed is in a sesame sprout, those sesame seeds are seen above it."
O beloved, it is seen in eight divisions according to its distribution upon the earth:
the root, the stem, the branch, the leaf, and likewise the flower, the fruit, the seed, and the oil; these they perceive as being equivalent to sesame.
Everything dissolves into the seed; the seed follows the body.
In this way, O Goddess, Māyā envelops the all-pervading Śiva within the *puryaṣṭaka*. 12.
O Goddess, this pervasion is entirely and completely [established] by the will of Śiva;
having meditated upon Śiva as omnipresent and situated within the interval between desire and the cessation of desire. (13)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Paramarahasya*, within the *Niruttaravāda* of the *Bhairavasrotas*.
There is no drinking of animal flesh, nor indeed sprinkling, nor likewise any ritual observance.
What is the use of conduct? What are the bonds, and who is remembered as the bound soul (paśu)? || 1 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said: As long as the distinction of ignorance exists, the bonds of worldly existence arise from it;
but having known the object of knowledge from the state of the Guru, they manifest the characteristic [of liberation] directly.
At that very time, the one whose self is disciplined, like a bird released from its bond, dissolves through practice within the interval of the exhaustion of the wick of attachment. (3)
Just as many drops of water cast into vessels of iron that have been thoroughly heated go to destruction upon falling [into them],
so too does [the mind] perish when it falls into the void which is of the nature of consciousness.
Just as a great mass of iron, blazing according to its nature and accompanied by sparks, gradually attains a state of coolness at the time when its heat has subsided; || 5 ||
Just as a flame, when its fuel is exhausted, dissolves into that blazing state which is free from disease and where no form exists; || 6 ||
One is liberated from the "ash-insect," yet fire is no longer seen;
in the suṣumṇā, the perception of sensory objects is no longer observed.
In the same way, nothing whatsoever is perceived at the commencement of Śiva;
yet, in his state as a physical body (piṇḍastha), childhood is not seen during his period of old age. (8)

When the functioning [of the mind] has dissolved and one has emerged, being free from limiting adjuncts and subject to no further influence, everything is absorbed into the ocean of space; one should not think of anything at all.
Because he does not think of anything at all, he is neither deluded nor destroyed;
having the form of space in its constant presence, that meditation on existence destroys [the notion of] existence.
When [the mind] is exhausted through the power of ego-identification, like the cloudless sky, the liberated one, whose self is disciplined, moves about like the wind in the atmosphere. (11)
No lapses exist for one who possesses a mind that has been extinguished; like the removal of impurity, liberation is perceived directly. 12.
Liberation, liberation, again liberation—liberation is not the casting off of the physical body;
it is neither the upward departure nor likewise the downward compression.
Indeed, there is the breaking of the wheel, misfortune, and upheaval along with the winds;
because of that, those who know reality suffer. But the teaching resides solely within the body.
When the state of affliction has ceased, consciousness is eternal, all-pervading, and auspicious. (15)
The Goddess said: "O Lord, I have been bewildered in this thicket; tell me that which destroys delusion.
You have spoken of the appearance of space—does it exist by virtue of a specific location?"
O Lord, why is it that even that which transcends form exists in the form of the *piṇḍastha* state?
Speak these words of Aghora to dispel this terrible doubt of mine. (17)
The illustrious Bhairava said: This place is possessed of a great knot and is utterly deluded by Mahāmāyā;
it is the domain of the Kāṇḍilī lineage, situated within the powerful station of karma.
If one’s desire arises toward the Self as consisting of mere bliss, that state is being liberated; however, it is certain that this is not the [proper] method. (19)
In the movement of the [supreme] state, that which consists of the bliss of mortals, situated within the eightfold internal divisions, is presided over by the power of will (icchā-śakti). || 20 ||
The power of will is merged in Śiva; therefore, one should abandon that state.
O beloved, one should take refuge in the Lord who abides in form, the reality that is Śiva.
Formless, exhausted of all [duality], devoid of coming and going, unerring, liberated from everything, it abides in the state that is beyond the range of the senses. || 22 ||

The path has been explained in four ways, up to the definition of the "body" (piṇḍa). When the body, whose nature is perishable and combustible, has perished, whose body, state, and sequence [would there be]? (23)
As long as there is a body within another lump [of matter], so long does consciousness have its characteristic mark;
once it has dissolved, by way of the path of emptiness, where is the gift, and where is the action? (24)
Those four castes exist only so long as one does not find the reality;
once this supreme reality is known, all distinctions of birth vanish.
O Dear One, the power whose form is memory is the Lord Bhairava;
Krodha is Kālāgnirudra, and likewise Māyā is Moha. (26)
Through my own conduct, I have experienced waves of worldly enjoyment and the play of Rudra; yet, due to the great bond of this miserable saṃsāra, death awaits me in the abode of Bhairava. || 27 ||
Śānta? Śīhā? Likewise, O Nanda, sexual union is the charioteer Piṇḍa;
wandering is the divine chariot, and Kālabhairava is the final destination. 28.
Whatever aggregate of ritual action there is, all that is impelled by Śiva;
it is the power whose form is unperceived, flowing in an uninterrupted stream. || 29 ||
For the sake of the play of both, there is an abiding in the three worlds.
She whose delight consists of the five elements is garlanded by the fivefold elements; woven with five colors, she manifests in manifold forms. (31)

The multiplicity and the various distinctions that have arisen consist of many different mantras; for mantras are indeed the names of deities, numbering in the tens of millions and beyond counting. (32)
The universe, consisting of the five elements, dissolves again into those five;
one should always consume these five, and never anything devoid of them. (33)
Adorned with five colors, it depicts the variegated ocean of existence;
therein are gathered all women, men, and those born of animal wombs.
Various medicines, the Ṛkṣa mountains, forest trees, lakes, sacred fords, rivers, gardens, and pasturelands for grass. || 35 ||
O beautiful lady, the activity of the five elements is never seen as identical;
that [activity] is seen in the mouth of the father and the mouth of the son. (36)
A mother and a daughter, as well as brothers born of the same womb,
possess a resemblance like that of a tree to its trunk, and likewise water to water.
On a mountain peak, one peak does not appear as identical to another; likewise, a river is not seen as similar to [another] river, and they know a flower to be like [another] flower. (38)
Thus, the fivefold [manifestation] at its root is presided over by Śiva and Śakti; there the Lord sports, expands, rejoices, speaks, and performs action. (39)
In one place it consists of servitude; in another, it is destitute of wealth;
in some places it is full of disease, O Rudra, and in others, it is long-lasting suffering.
In one place he becomes immoral, and in another virtuous; in one place he is a vidyādhara with a beautiful form, and in another a fool with a deformed appearance. || 41 ||
In one place he is a serpent, in another an insect, in another a bird or a monkey; sometimes he is the light of the sun, moon, and fire, and sometimes he is death or life.
Thus, this cage of beings is manifold, variegated, and diverse, through the differentiation and non-differentiation of the five elements by the mind. (43)
By whom it is known—[he who is] otherwise [than this] is bound like an animal;
[he who] stands neither in purity nor in impurity... || 44 ||
On one side are all existing things, on the other side is the ultimate reality;
on one side is the path to Brahman, and on the other is the Lord of Umā alone.
O auspicious one who consists of all Brahman, that which is of the nature of certainty must be known. || 46 ||
When the Knowable is known, liberation occurs; otherwise, there is the bondage of worldly existence.
This does not happen through sacrifices, gifts, or the status of a donor, nor by traveling to sacred pilgrimage sites.
Neither indeed by leaping from a cliff, nor by fire or within water, nor by the kṛcchra or atikṛcchra penances, nor even by the cāndrāyaṇa vow [is such a goal attained]. || 48 ||
Liberation comes through fasting; liberation does not come from eating alms-food. Always keep the mind free from agitation throughout the night. (49)
The family (kula) is endowed with the eightfold [perfections] such as the seat of the destruction of evil and so forth, and it is pervaded by the assembly (saṅgha). || 50 ||
It is joined with the eight Nāgas and the planets, manifested as the eight directions;
it stands between the left, the right, and the center, situated within the interval of Kulakaula.
The thirty-three crores of gods were made into a single line;
everything dissolved from the body, as previously stated and enjoined.
The knower of yoga should constantly worship his own *liṅga* with an unchanging mind; whatever object the mind is enveloped by, he should cause that very thing to be offered within the *manas*.
One should meditate on that which is peaceful as being peaceful through the very nature of each respective thing;
for it has no origination in its own true form, being turned toward all directions.
Is that Śiva indeed Keśava? He is Brahmā and he is Sūrya as well.
He is Yama, the consumer of hearts; for by his mere sight, he destroys all sins.

One is liberated from that [sin] by the mere touch of those who are known as knowers of Brahman; even the body attains purity through such contact, so what need be said of one who is in their immediate proximity? (56)
"He should release [the disciple] from conversation, bodily contact, and the touch of limbs; he is the destroyer of the flood of fire.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the venerable Rasendracūḍāmaṇi.
The Goddess said:
O God, it is certain that [this] is the destroyer of great existence (saṃsāra) in every respect;
it must be grasped within my heart, for it is indeed ungraspable by the beast-like followers of Bharata.
One should know the supreme *vaṃ*, which is other than emptiness and born from emptiness; for whose desire is it seen in the three times in manifold ways? (2)
"All this is of the nature of Śiva; the Lord is Śiva and not otherwise.
O Lord, how is it that the three worlds are seen as distinct from him? (3)

O Protector, the diversity [of teachings] is profound due to the injunctions regarding the meaning of mantra and tantra; there is neither favor nor suppression, neither cruelty, nor devotion, or even deceit. (4)
Whose notion is it that "she is dead," or who has actually entered a state of being lifeless?
To the very one who is the destroyer of death, who indeed could be more "deathless" than you?
O Lord, by whom could he be impelled, and for whose sake would death be certain?
For the eternally risen God, whose destruction of intellect could there be? (6)
The multiplicity of existence is opposed to the nature of oneness.
Śrī Bhairava said: Those who have died go to the terrible darkness within the supreme void.
He likewise [honored] the deities and the sacred fords situated in secret abodes.
The mountains and rivers, the earth girdled by the seven oceans, the various beings of the sea, and whatever others arise as worms; || 9 ||
The Nāgas, the Grahas, the Dakṣas, those who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth;
likewise, the Pīṭhas, Upapīṭhas, Sandohas, Nirjharas, and Anirjharas. || 10 ||
Knots, thousands of knots, marrow, intellect, blood, and a lump of flesh—nothing at all is found in the corpse-like body. (11)
There is neither pleasure nor pain, nor even bliss, nor indeed any cultivation;
it is a state devoid of desire for knowledge, where the Lord is formless.
It is not a cause for the measurement of time, free from attachment and devoid of clinging; it is without support, without exertion, become void, and has the nature of Śiva.

Through the destruction of perception, that consciousness becomes lifeless and takes on the form of space; when that consciousness, whose abode is the void, is agitated, it then attains a physical body.
One should enter into awakening alone, perceiving the knowledge of the mass;
abiding eternally in an unshakable form, one who knows the end of the *kula* has the appearance of space. (15)
That [state] of the non-family (akula) is seen everywhere and yet is not seen;
by whomsoever it is known without delusion, by him Bhairava is truly known. 16.
Just as the edge of a column of smoke, when exhausted, is seen within the sky as formless and dissolved, so too is the embodied soul like the sky. 17.
When that very lump of clay has been completely crushed right here,
its residue proceeds to exist only very gradually.

Is water not being contemplated? Tell me, O embodied one, is there anything else within the lineage? All this is the manifestation of the object of consciousness; knowledge is the domain of ignorance. 19.
In the supportless state, in the void, devoid of all undertakings,
in the firm and supreme abode within the dissolution of Śiva and Śakti.
Beyond the sphere of names, free from birth and death—into that [state] goes this entire universe, whatever is composed of the five elements. (21)
Free from conceptual proliferation, rich in grace, stable, and indeed constant,
it is at one time manifold in form as the sixty-four Bhairavas.
Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Gocarī, and likewise Śākinī; as well as the Kiṃkaras, Gaṇas, Gandharvas, Ṛṣis, and Apsarases. || 23 ||
There are medicinal herbs, minerals, ores, and the origins of the five metals;
as well as kinnaras, bhūtas, piśācas, worms, insects, and reptiles. (24)
The five elements are the great elements (mahābhūtas), and the principles (tattvas) are thirty-six in number;
likewise, there are one hundred and eight principles situated within the intervals between those principles.
The root is the element, likewise the seed; it is both empty and non-empty.
Thus, O Umā, the manifestation of saṃsāra is indeed honored by me.
I never wander alone; there is no state of emptiness. Everything consists of everything, and within that, you are found by me. (27)
Sometimes such a universe is seen within the Supreme Self—
entirely composed of the terrible equilibrium of all things, an ocean of the union of powers.
O beautiful lady, by your mere agitation, the cosmic egg was raised up;
yet when it dissolves, O fair one, the universe does not perish along with those two.
When one contemplates nothing at all—that which is empty and without support—then, O Goddess, by not contemplating anything, one neither perishes nor becomes deluded. (30)
In that state, there is neither bliss nor power, nor even Śiva;
there is no perception, nor indeed existence, nor non-existence, nor conceptual construction.
It is solely emptiness and sound; there is no second—this is the certainty. || 32 ||
O God, this secret has been told, which was guarded by the Dānavas; it was not previously revealed by Śukra for the sake of the Asuras, nor was he made aware of it. (33)
O Lord, for whom would there be initiation, or whose lineage (kula) should one purify?
For Īśa is established everywhere; who is to be purified, and who attains perfection?
There is no binding with fetters, nor is there any characteristic of the conduct of the *samaya*; then, in the sequence of teacher and disciple, what is to be done and what is the purpose? (35)
"O Lord Śaṅkara, a delusion has been produced; indeed, I have been led astray. (36)
For one whose mind is exhausted of conceptual construction, what is the purpose of initiation, and for whom?
[It is for] that person who possesses conceptual construction, who is subject to rebirth, and who is defiled. (37)
What initiation is there for one who is stained by passion and the like?
Having cultivated such a state of being as has been described to you, [one attains] that which is the supreme lord of states of being. (38)

Meditation, worship and the like, recitation, the rites ending with the fire-oblation (homa), and the ritual placement (nyāsa)—these he should show to those desiring to ascend to the station that is the cause of invocation. (39)
Liberation arises from vision, for [the Self] is all-pervading and free from affliction;
meditation, worship, and so forth—all that originates from conceptual construction (saṅkalpa).
Initiation devoid of conceptual construction becomes the initiation of initiations;
liberated from both existence and non-existence, one should conduct oneself according to the practice of liberation.
They obscure the supreme truth with logic and trouble people in other ways; thus they display their scholarship in the scriptures, arrogant in their pride regarding the Vedas. (42)
Otherwise, the world—which is in essence free of waves—suffers in another way;
for otherwise, those possessed by delusion apply the instruction in yet another way. (43)
Otherwise one makes firmness in meditation, yet otherwise it is not firm;
otherwise there is supreme power, and otherwise people suffer.
One should abandon speech, cavil, and the mental impressions that define the boundaries of words and their meanings;
for they say that logic is no protection, whereas the supreme Śiva is the ultimate refuge for protection. 45.
Non-duality is the eternal practice; the dualistic sign is insentient.
A sign made of wood or stone, or even one made of gold, is merely an external object for the Creator.
Nor indeed, O Goddess, does that which is made of clay, nor that born of jewels, nor that produced from crystal and the like—being insentient—provide protection for consciousness in this matter. (47)

O Goddess of gods, one should meditate in every way upon the Liṅga in which the moving and the unmoving are dissolved; for the sake of protection, this state of non-duality should exist everywhere. (48)
Through practice over many successive births, one attains clear realization;
yet, even without the beauty of such realization, when one is commanded by the Guru, [the goal is attained]. 49.
Then he attains liberation; otherwise, from wandering [in saṃsāra], there is fear.
He should constantly realize non-duality (advaita) as being of the nature of Śiva in all states. 50.
Non-duality is the supreme dharma; non-duality is the supreme state.
Non-duality is the firm liberation; non-duality is characterized by enjoyment.
Non-duality with its instruction, non-duality of the noble and the ignoble—there is no rule of duality or non-duality; one should enter the state of Śambhu.
The object of practice, which is equanimous, all-pervading, and empty, is cultivated as the means of accomplishment;
though it may be non-duality, I salute that duality which is the fire-drill of the Kula.

The teacher, the fire, and likewise the mantra—there is no conceptualization of division among these; nor is there non-duality [between them]. This is the definitive conclusion of this scripture. (54)
Because the names and the instructions are clearly perceived,
through the distinction of the name and the paryanka, they are likewise of one essence in a single way.
All those who violate the teacher’s bed wander as beasts;
those who are doubtful regarding knowledge wander, deluded by the state of ignorance. (56)
They will not know the supreme state by which liberation from bondage is attained;
some call it the *haṃsa*, while others call it the living *praṇava*.
Some worship the Bindu, others likewise the Nāda; some worship Śakti and the Supreme Amṛta; and some worship the Supreme State, the bliss beyond Śakti. || 58 ||

Some [say it] consists of the five voids; some [say it is] the dissolution of sound and so forth; some [say it is] Śaiva, likewise Daiva; and some [say it is] Jyotis, the sphere of the celestial bodies. (59)
Some [describe it as] free from the six waves; others as the tip of the uvula; some as the *mātṛkā*, the digits (*kalā*), and the bindu; and others as the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) beyond touch.
Some, however, [speak of] one deficient in senses, while others [speak of] one endowed with all the senses;
some say that the self is established within the Supreme Self. (61)
Some [say] that Prakṛti is Puruṣa; some say it is sixfold; some say it is Prāṇa, as well as Buddhi; and some say it is indeed Dhairya.
Some [saw it] resembling a blazing fire, some like the sun,
some like a strand of wool, and others like a firefly.
Some [saw it] as that very intuition (*pratibhā*), some as pure as crystal;
some [saw it] as the tip of a hair, and some as having the luster of a row of sunbeams. (64)
Some [saw] his form as consisting of shadow; some [saw it] as being free from the sun;
some [saw it] as standing without support; and some [saw it] as endowed with the fruits of sacrifice.
Some describe it as being without waves; some as having the characteristic of expansion;
some as ending at the limit of sexual pleasure; and some as having its range in the ultimate finality.

Some [describe him as] delusion, some as a magician; some as one who is entirely free from all [attributes]; some as possessing characteristics and lacking characteristics; and some as desireless and free from affliction.
Some [perceive] the state of heat, others the surge of bliss;
some perceive the pleasure of the sense objects, and others the space within the wheel.
Some [say it is] beyond the *dvādaśānta*; some [say it is] adorned by the wheel of space (*khe-cakra*);
some [say it is] consisting of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*); and some [say it is] the state at the limit of resonance (*ghoṣa*).
Some [regard him] as one who rejoices in the self, while others are proponents of non-self;
likewise, some regard him as God and so forth, while others are proponents of non-God.
Some [regard it as] the complete supreme [mantra], some as the supreme syllable of the mantra;
some as consisting of fifty letters, and some as ending with the fire of Kāśā.
Some regard it as the swing of bliss, some as the characteristic of freedom from delusion,
some as having the form of deep sleep, and others as the support of the fourth state (turya).

Some [describe it] as possessing qualities (saguṇa), some as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); some as resembling the wind, some as the state of Sanatkumāra’s bliss, and some indeed as being free from all affliction (anāmaya).

Some [regard] the reality (tattva) as eternal bliss; likewise, some as having the nature of absolute freedom (svātantrya); some as devoid of manifestation (prabhāva), yet established among the principles (tattva). || 74 ||
Some say that Viṣṇu is Nārāyaṇa, the unborn;
others indeed say he is the eternal form of light of Vāsudeva.
Some [regard] the Buddha as that which is to be known; some [regard] consciousness alone; some, having become thus empty; and some [regard] nirvana alone. || 76 ||
Some [describe] the dharmadhātu as such; some [describe] the transformation through the three times;
likewise, some [describe] eternal bliss, and others [describe] the unstruck sound (anāhata). 77.
Some say it is free from conceptual construction; some say it is the regulator of all beings;
some say it is called the *praṇava*; and some say it is established in direct perception.
Some say it exists, some say it does not exist, and some maintain that it is devoid of both; some say it is such-and-such, while others remain established in bliss. (79)
Some say it is the All-pervasive Lord, others the Witness, and still others the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
some say it is that which transcends space, and others that which is born of pure discrimination.
Some proponents maintain that this is the power (śakti) which possesses those attributes; others hold it to be the coiled power (kuṇḍalinī-śakti) resting upon the place of birth. 81.

Some have described *śakti* as vigor, strength, and enthusiasm; others say it is the power residing in the place of birth (*janmasthāna*), which spreads to the cavity of the palate (*tālurandhra*). (82)
Some worship the *mātṛ-tattva* as all the deities;
others, with purified minds, perceive it as situated between the moon, the sun, and fire.
Some [assert] the mind, others likewise the feeler; some the agent is prescribed.
Such and other [views] are established through millions of distinctions. (84)
It could not be calculated even by hundreds of many millions. || 85 ||
O Sage, by what path is that stainless [reality] to be grasped along with its instruction?
Tell me the characteristic of rest; O Hara, abandon the distinctions of number. (86)
Where no grasping exists nor any relinquishing, where the mind is not found, there,
upon attaining the state of bliss, one is immersed in the bliss beyond bliss.
When the state beyond joy is attained, the conceit that seizes upon birth no longer exists; for him there is neither name nor clan, nor caste, nor even birth itself. (88)
In this case, time does not exist, nor is anything to be deliberated upon ever perceived;
whatever kind of entity appears, it must exist together with that very appearance.
One whose inner being is freed from the dualities of sight, mind, desire, and volition attains supreme bliss, the face of the Full Path that destroys darkness. (90)
Since there is nothing equal to that, it cannot be described; yet the wise speak thus for the sake of upholding their own scriptures. (91)
The dense thicket of doubt is real; he who, having attained knowledge, understands that which is capable of liberating bound beings (paśu) is a wise man. 92.
His intellect is a great attainment; the others are merely intermediate obstacles.
Thus ends the fifth chapter on the *uddeśa* of the *Devarasra* in the *Śrīparamarahasya*.
This [work] titled *Nirūpavadam* is completed; may it be auspicious.
